title: The Investor-Ready Story Audit
subtitle: Score whether your founder narrative is clear, credible, and specific enough to raise capital and win clients before you spend a dollar amplifying it.

questions.text: Read your homepage headline out loud. What does it actually say?

answers.label: It uses words like 'leading,' 'innovative,' or 'best-in-class' with no numbers attached
It describes what we do but has no proof point or metric
It includes a number but it is a market size stat, not something we own
It includes a specific metric that is uniquely ours: users, revenue, or outcomes we drove
The first sentence contains a number no other company can claim, and a reader could verify it in under a minute

questions.text: Your three strongest proof points. How would a skeptical investor react to them?

answers.label: They are qualitative: 'clients love us,' 'amazing traction,' 'market-leading'
They are real numbers but common ones: revenue, users, growth percentage alone
They have numbers but I would need a follow-up sentence to explain the context
Each one is specific, contextualized, and tells a before-and-after story
Each one is checkable, uniquely ours, and lands a category claim the moment you read it

questions.text: Go count the adjectives in the first paragraph of your pitch or homepage. What do you find?

answers.label: Five or more adjectives describing quality, with no numbers to back any of them
Three or four adjectives, one metric buried later in the page
Two adjectives and one number, but the number is a market size, not a company outcome
One adjective and at least one specific number we own in the first two sentences
No adjectives doing the work. A specific number does the job every adjective would have attempted

low.headline: Your proof points are invisible right now.
low.text: Words like 'leading' and 'innovative' cost nothing to say, so they prove nothing. A reader's brain files them as noise before the next sentence starts. You have real numbers. The work is getting them into the first paragraph.
steps: Pull up your homepage. Count every adjective in the first paragraph. Ask which three can be replaced by a specific number you actually own.
List your five best outcomes for customers, in numbers, with a time window: '$40k to $130k/mo in 90 days' is a sentence nobody else can say.
Write one sentence that only you can say. No other company can claim it. Test it by searching for it online.

mid.headline: You have numbers, but they are not doing enough work yet.
mid.text: Having metrics is the floor, not the ceiling. The founders closing rounds right now do not just show growth. They show numbers that land a category claim the moment you read them. Context and uniqueness are what separate your number from every other founder's deck.
steps: For each metric you use, ask: could a competitor say this exact sentence? If yes, it is not a differentiator yet.
Add a before-and-after frame to your strongest proof point. A two-state number with a time window is significantly stronger than a single-state one.
Move your best number into the first sentence of your pitch, your bio, and your homepage. If it is buried on slide eight, it is not working.

high.headline: Your specificity is a real asset. Now sharpen the frame.
high.text: You are ahead of most founders on this. The numbers are there and they are yours. The next step is making sure each one lands a category claim, not just a progress update. A number that says 'we are growing' is different from a number that says 'we are inevitable.'
steps: Review your proof points and ask which ones tell an investor why your category is winning right now, not just that your company is working.
Add one sentence after your strongest metric that names the category shift it reflects.
Test your homepage with three people who do not know your company. What category do they put you in after 30 seconds?

questions.text: A partner who has seen 200 decks this year asks why your category is inevitable right now. What do you say?

answers.label: I lead with our growth numbers. I have not built a category timing argument beyond that
I can explain the trend but I rely on macro stats investors have already seen
I have a timing argument but it takes me a few minutes to get to it in a conversation
I can state in one sentence why this category is opening up right now, and it is specific to this moment
My timing narrative connects a specific shift to a specific opening, and investors have told me it is the clearest version they have heard

questions.text: How does your pitch handle the AI question, whether AI touches your product or not?

answers.label: I avoid the AI framing entirely. It feels like a stretch for what we build
I mention AI because investors expect it, but I have not stress-tested whether the connection is thin
I have a real AI angle but I lead with product first and bring it in later
If AI genuinely touches our product, I lead with it. I know investors spot a thin connection in the first two minutes
My AI framing, or my deliberate non-AI positioning, is a specific narrative choice I can defend with concrete examples

questions.text: Non-AI venture funding adjusted for inflation sits below 2020 levels. Does your pitch account for the market your investors are actually operating in?

answers.label: I reference total VC market size as context for the opportunity, not the actual raise environment
I know conditions are tighter but I have not adjusted my pitch language to reflect it
I acknowledge the environment when asked but I do not lead with it
I can articulate the funding picture in my specific category and how my timing fits inside it
My pitch explicitly names the gap between the macro VC headlines and my category's actual raise conditions, and positions us inside that gap

low.headline: Growing 3x does not close rounds on its own anymore.
low.text: Every founder in a live deal right now has a growth number. The ones getting checks can also tell you why their category is inevitable at this specific moment. That is the argument your pitch is missing.
steps: Write one sentence that answers: why is this category winning right now, not in three years? Put a specific date, stat, or event in it.
Research the actual funding picture in your category. Not total VC, but deals in your vertical over the last four quarters. That is the room you are pitching into.
If AI genuinely touches your product, move that framing into the first two minutes. If it does not, decide now how you will address the question when it comes.

mid.headline: You have a timing story. It needs to land faster.
mid.text: The argument is there, but if it takes several minutes to reach, it is not working. Investors writing checks in this environment are pattern-matching on category inevitability before they are halfway through your deck. The timing narrative has to be front-loaded.
steps: Write a two-sentence version of your category timing argument. If you cannot compress it, the logic is not tight enough yet.

Pull out the macro stats you are using and ask: have the investors you are meeting already seen these? Replace any stat that has been in the news cycle with one specific to your category or deal data.
Move the timing argument to slide two or your opening monologue. It should land before the product demo.

high.headline: Your category narrative is a real edge. Use it as one.
high.text: Most founders can tell you why their company is working. You can also tell them why this specific moment is the right one for the category. That combination is what gets you into the second meeting. Make sure it is the first thing you say.
steps: Ask the last three investors you met: what did you hear that you had not heard before? Their answer tells you which part of your timing narrative is actually landing.
Write a one-paragraph version of your category timing argument that a non-technical client could read and understand. If you cannot, you are still using insider framing.
Test whether your timing argument works in two completely different contexts: a VC meeting and a client sales call. The core logic should hold in both.

questions.text: When you publish on LinkedIn, where does most of your time and attention go?

answers.label: Almost entirely on the company page. That is the brand we are building
Split roughly evenly between my personal profile and the company page
Mostly my personal profile, but I repurpose most posts to the company page as well
My personal profile first, with a real point of view. The company page gets what is left
My personal profile is the primary channel. I have watched it consistently outperform the company page and I plan around that

questions.text: Look at the last post you published. What does it actually say about how you think?

answers.label: It is a product announcement or company update with nothing about my perspective
It is industry news with some added context but no clear opinion from me
It has a point of view but I softened it to stay safe
It makes a specific claim in my voice that a reader who follows me would recognize as mine
It states a position I would defend in a room full of people who disagree, backed by a specific number or story

questions.text: How do you know whether your content is actually working?

answers.label: I track impressions and likes. That is what the dashboard shows me
I watch for comments and shares. That feels like real engagement
I pay attention to DMs and whether people mention the post in live conversations
I track which posts lead to discovery calls or inbound from the right people
I can tell you which of my last ten posts booked a call and which did not, and I have changed my content mix based on that

low.headline: You are the distribution. The brand page is what you send people to after they already trust you.
low.text: Company page reach on LinkedIn sits at roughly 5% of the feed, and it has dropped about 60% since 2024. The time you are putting into that channel is mostly invisible. The post that books the call comes from a person, not a logo.
steps: For the next four weeks, put every piece of content on your personal profile first. Track which one books a conversation.
Write one post this week with a specific number and one sentence that tells the reader exactly what you think. Not what the data suggests. What you think.
Pull up your last ten posts and count how many include a real opinion versus an industry observation. That ratio tells you what you are actually optimizing for.

mid.headline: You are posting in the right place. Now make the posts do real work.
mid.text: Personal profile is the right call. The gap is between content that gets attention and content that books calls. Those are not the same posts. A 200,000-impression post that books zero calls and a 1,100-impression post that books three are telling you something. The one that books calls is the one worth studying.
steps: Go back through your last ten posts and note which ones generated direct outreach: DMs, email mentions, call bookings. That is your signal.
Take the post that did worst on impressions but best on real engagement. Write another one like it.
Stop publishing anything that could have been written by someone who is not you. Every post should have at least one sentence a reader could only get from following you specifically.

high.headline: You are running the right scoreboard. Most founders are not.
high.text: Tracking which content books calls instead of which content gets impressions is the thing almost nobody does. You are already doing it. The question now is whether the content that works for you is also building the warm room you will need before your next raise.
steps: Map your last 90 days of content against your pipeline. Which posts show up in conversations where a client or investor already knows who you are before you reach out?
Ask yourself: if someone has been reading your posts for six months, what do they believe about you that they would not believe about a competitor? That is the brand you are actually building.
Take one post that booked a call and write a sharper version of the same argument. What would you say differently now that you know it works?

categories.name: The Warm Room Before the Ask

questions.text: Think about the last time you sent a cold email to an investor or enterprise buyer. How warm was the room before it landed?

answers.label: Cold. They had no exposure to me or my thinking before that email arrived
We had one mutual connection but no direct engagement or context
They had seen something about us, a press mention or a conference, but no personal connection to my work
They had read something I wrote or heard me speak. They had a prior reason to respond
They reached out to me first, or the cold email went to someone who already knew my thinking from following my content

questions.text: The founders who move fastest through a round almost always share one thing: the investor already knows them before the cold email. How are you building that?

answers.label: I am not. I send decks and wait. The content strategy is separate from the raise
I post occasionally but I have not connected my content to who I want in my cap table
I know which investors I am targeting and I engage with their content, but I do not know if they have seen mine
I publish a consistent point of view that investors in my target list could find if they searched for founders in my space
I can name three investors or clients who know my thinking before I have ever sent them a deck, because they have engaged with something I said publicly

questions.text: If you are raising or pushing hard on enterprise sales in the next six months, how many people on your target list already know who you are?

answers.label: Fewer than five. Most of my outreach will be cold
Maybe ten to fifteen, through networking events and conferences
Twenty or more, but most of the connection is a handshake, not real familiarity with my thinking
A clear subset of my target list has followed my work, seen me speak, or engaged with something I have written
The majority of my first-round outreach will go to people who have already had a reason to trust me before I ask for anything

low.headline: You are building the pitch before you have built the room.
low.text: The warm room is harder to manufacture than any stat in the deck, and it cannot be built the week before you go out to raise. The founders who move fastest through a round almost always have investors who already know them. That familiarity does not come from one great cold email.
steps: List the ten investors or clients you most want in your next round or deal. Find out what they read, where they speak, and what they have said publicly in the last 90 days.
Start publishing one specific point of view per week that the people on that list would have a reason to read. Not about your company. About the category and the problem.
Engage with their public work before you ever send a deck. Comment with something specific. Share with a real sentence about why. Make yourself recognizable before you make the ask.

mid.headline: You are networking, but not necessarily building familiarity with how you think.
mid.text: A handshake at a conference is not the same as an investor who knows your view on the market. The latter is what converts a cold email into a fast reply. The difference is whether they have read something from you, not just met you.
steps: Audit your existing network against your target raise list. Which of those relationships are based on your thinking versus your title or a mutual introduction?
Send one piece of content to five people on your target list with a specific note about why you wrote it. Not a pitch. Just the thinking.
Publish one post this month that takes a specific position on something happening in your category. The investors you want to know you should recognize your view on it.

high.headline: You are building the warm room while everyone else is writing cold outreach templates.
high.text: This is the edge almost nobody is playing. Keep building it. The goal is to reach a place where the cold email you send is really just a formal first step to someone who already thinks of you as worth a conversation.
steps: Map which content has generated the most inbound from your target investor or client profile. Double down on that format and topic, not the content that got the most impressions overall.
Ask three people in your target list directly: what do they associate with your name when they hear it? Their answer tells you whether the narrative you think you are building is actually landing.

Set a concrete goal: before you go out to raise or push on enterprise clients, you want a specific number of people from your target list to have engaged with something you published. Pick the number and work backward from it.

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: In 30 minutes I'll show you which two gaps to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing.

answers.label: Actively raising a round in the next 90 days
Funded and pushing to win more enterprise clients
Building narrative before going to market
Scaling GTM as a funded founder
